story:
A fir from the American West has become Wisconsin's champion of its kind in front of a small-town cemetery office. The Wisconsin DNR champion register measured this white fir at Greenwood Cemetery in Monroe at 2.62 metres round and 25.6 metres tall, with a crown about 20 metres one way and 17 the other.

White fir is a western species, so somebody planted this one. The register does not say who or when, and we have found nothing that does. What gives it away is the colour of its needles, a soft blue-grey that is the white fir's own.

It does not stand alone. Just west of the same office grows the register's champion tulip tree, 28.2 metres tall, so one short stop in Monroe gives you two of the state's record trees within a few steps of each other. The fir is the shorter and the slimmer of the pair, and the only one that keeps its colour through the winter.

The register is the only source for either tree, and it does not record when they were measured. Greenwood is a working cemetery run by its association; come in daylight. If you know when the fir was planted, tell us.

story:
The biggest tulip tree in the Wisconsin DNR champion register grows beside a cemetery office in Monroe, and it stands 28.2 metres tall. The register measured a trunk 3.18 metres round and a crown about 17 metres across, just west of the Greenwood Cemetery office. In front of the same office stands a second state champion, a white fir, so the two are one stop.

The leaves are the giveaway, cut off square at the tip where most leaves come to a point, so each one looks like a saddle. In late spring the tree flowers, green and orange cups shaped like tulips, but they open high in the crown and are easy to miss from the ground. Autumn is the season to come. The leaves turn a clear, even yellow, one of the most reliable autumn displays of any tree.

As with the fir, the register is the only record. It gives no measurement date and no age, and we found no one who has written about either tree. The cemetery is in town, about 45 minutes by car south-west of Madison; visit in daylight and keep to the paths. If you know when these two were planted, tell us.

story:
La Crosse named a trail after this tree. The Cottonwood Trail through the La Crosse River Marsh takes its name from the giant beside it, an eastern cottonwood that the Wisconsin DNR champion register measures at 7.92 metres round. That is a waist of nearly eight metres, on a tree 29.6 metres tall with a crown about 30 metres one way and 25 the other.

The register scores a tree by adding its trunk in inches, its height in feet and a quarter of its crown, and this cottonwood comes to 432 points. For scale, the two cottonwoods on our Chicago page, both from the forest preserves there, are under six metres round, though both are taller than this one.

You reach it on foot. The marsh trails start from Myrick Park, a city park about ten minutes' drive from downtown, and the Cottonwood Trail is unpaved. Neither the register nor anyone else we found gives the distance from the park entrance to the tree; a loop of about two kilometres runs through this part of the marsh.

Nobody has dated it, and the register does not say when it was measured. It is recently seen, though. A visitor recorded it at the spot at the end of October 2026. If you know how old it is, tell us.

story:
Wisconsin's champion sycamore grows next to a post office in downtown Fond du Lac, and it is wider than it is tall. The Wisconsin DNR champion register measured a crown about 31 metres one way and 26.5 the other, on a tree 25.3 metres high, over a trunk 6.48 metres round. The register adds trunk inches, height in feet and a quarter of the crown, and the total comes to 361.5 points. The bark is what you notice first, mottled white.

Chicago's forest preserves grow their sycamores taller. The champion at Riverside Lawn on our Chicago page reaches 41.5 metres. But it is 3.91 metres round, and this downtown tree carries more than two and a half metres more around the trunk. Height is one way to be big; this one went sideways.

We should say plainly what we do not know. The register is the only source, it does not name which post office, and it does not say when it measured the tree. A visitor recorded a sycamore near the pin in July 2023. We read it as a tree on the public side, seen from the street, but its exact spot is not confirmed, and the pin is approximate. If you know the spot, or its age, tell us.

story:
One limb of this catalpa is so heavy that it rests on concrete blocks. The tree stands thirty yards south of the library on the University of Wisconsin-Platteville campus, and the Wisconsin DNR champion register ranks it the biggest northern catalpa in the state, 6.71 metres round and 28 metres tall, with a crown about 24 metres one way and 22.5 the other.

That girth needs a footnote. The trunk splits between one and one and a half metres above the ground, so the measurers could not take it at the usual height and went round at 36 inches instead. Treat the figure as approximate; the tree is enormous either way.

The best account of it is a re-measurement note from the register's curator, dated 25 August 2021. It describes the old champion with its trunk splitting low, its foliage still full, and the big west bough held up on its blocks. Somebody, at some point, decided this limb was worth propping rather than cutting, and the tree has carried on.

That 2021 note is also the latest word we have. Nobody has published an age for the tree, and the register does not say when the original measurement was made. If you have walked past the library recently, tell us how it is doing.

story:
Chestnut oak does not grow wild in Wisconsin, and the state's champion is a planted tree in an arboretum near Poynette. The Wisconsin DNR champion register ranks this one, at the MacKenzie Environmental Education Center, as the biggest of its kind in the state, at 1.78 metres round and 20.1 metres tall, with a narrow crown about 11 metres one way and under 8 the other.

Those are modest numbers for a champion, and we would rather say so than dress them up. Come for an oak a long way from home, not for a giant.

The centre's history is the more surprising part. It began as the State Game Farm and took its present name in 1971, and today it is run by the state's Department of Natural Resources as an education centre with a planted arboretum.

Two more register champions stand within about 250 metres, a sweet birch a few dozen metres away and a yellow buckeye north of the office, so the three make a short walk. The register is the only source for each and gives no measurement dates. Visiting hours and any fee were not confirmed, so check with the centre before the 40-minute drive north from Madison. If you know when the arboretum was planted, tell us.

story:
This sweet birch spreads a crown about 20 metres wide on a tree 21.3 metres tall, nearly as broad as it is high. It grows at the MacKenzie Environmental Education Center near Poynette, and the Wisconsin DNR champion register ranks it the biggest sweet birch in the state, with a trunk 2.16 metres round.

Sweet birch is a tree of the eastern United States, and like its two champion neighbours in this arboretum it was planted. Of the three, it has by far the widest crown. The chestnut oak, a few dozen metres away, spreads about 11 metres, the yellow buckeye about 13, and this birch about 20 one way and 17 the other.

The register places it at the west end of the western part of the arboretum, close to the oak. The buckeye stands north of the centre's office, a couple of hundred metres to the east, so the three make one short walk.

The ground has had more than one life. The centre was the State Game Farm until it was renamed in 1971, and the state's Department of Natural Resources now runs it for environmental education. The register is the only record of this tree. It gives no measurement date, and nobody has published an age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

story:
Wisconsin's champion yellow buckeye is filed in the state register under a name botanists have since set aside. The Wisconsin DNR champion register lists it as Aesculus octandra, an older name now treated as a synonym of Aesculus flava. Under either name, it is the biggest of its species the register knows.

It grows at the MacKenzie Environmental Education Center near Poynette, west of the sidewalk and north of the centre's office. The register measured a trunk 2.26 metres round and a height of 22.6 metres, with a compact crown about 13 metres one way and 12 the other. That makes it the tallest and the thickest of the three register champions in this arboretum, though the sweet birch at the west end spreads far wider.

Like the birch and the chestnut oak, it was planted. The centre started life as the State Game Farm and took its present name in 1971, and the arboretum the state's Department of Natural Resources keeps here is a planted collection, not a wild wood.

This is the easiest of the three to find, since it stands near the office, and a good place to start the short walk to the other two. The register is the only source for it and gives no measurement date or age. Hours and any fee were not confirmed, so check before you go. If you know when it went in, tell us.

story:
This black cherry stands 32 metres tall, 105 feet, beside the headquarters of the Kettle Moraine State Forest, and the Wisconsin DNR champion register ranks it the biggest of its species in the state. The register measured a trunk 2.74 metres round and a crown about 20 metres across in both directions, close to a circle.

Set it beside its rivals across the Illinois line. The champion black cherry of the Chicago forest preserves, on our Chicago page, is thicker at 3.35 metres round but shorter at 29.3 metres. A second-ranked cherry in Swallow Cliff Woods reaches 34.7 metres. Champion registers on both sides of the border score the whole tree, trunk, height and crown together, so the tallest does not always win.

The register's directions are simple. Park at the headquarters lot and use the walking paths. Its coordinates are rounded, so our pin is loose and the building is your best guide. The register names only the Kettle Moraine headquarters; we read that as the Southern Unit's, near Eagle, which the register itself does not confirm. A vehicle admission sticker is likely needed for cars in the state forest.

The register is the only source for this tree, with no measurement date and no age. If you have seen it, or know how old it is, tell us.

story:
This red pine stands 34.2 metres tall at the edge of a car park in a county park on Upper St. Croix Lake. The Wisconsin DNR champion register ranks it the biggest red pine in the state, with a trunk 2.63 metres round and a narrow crown about 12 metres across, a column rather than a spreading tree.

The comparison with Illinois is striking. The state champion red pine there, on a golf course on our Chicago page, is 19.5 metres tall and 2.07 metres round. This one is nearly 15 metres taller, and more than half a metre thicker round.

Lucius Woods County Park belongs to Douglas County and is open to day visitors, with a beach, a campground and a nature trail. The pine is easy to find without any of them. It stands at the south-west corner of the parking lot in the middle of the park, where the register puts it. The bark is plated and orange-brown, the red pine's colours.

Solon Springs is about 35 minutes by car south-east of Superior, and there is no public transport. The register is the only source for this tree and does not date its measurement. Nobody has published an age. If you know it, tell us.

story:
The Wisconsin DNR champion register measured this eastern white pine at 157 feet, 47.9 metres, and you can see it from a gravel road in the Nicolet National Forest. It stands east of Forest Road 2454, Huff Creek Road, with a trunk 3.96 metres round and a crown about 16 metres one way and 15 the other.

That height is the reason to make the drive. The tallest white pine on our Chicago page, the champion of the Cook County forest preserves, is 29.3 metres. This one is more than 18 metres taller, on a trunk well over a metre thicker. Its crown is narrow for that height, barely a third as wide as the tree is tall.

The tree is on US Forest Service land and costs nothing to see. You do not need to leave the road, and we do not describe a walking route to it. Forest roads like this one can close for the season, so check before you go. There is no public transport, and the nearest towns are some way off.

The register is the only source. The height is its measurement, not ours, and it does not say when it was taken. Nobody has published an age. If you know it, or have seen the tree recently, tell us.

story:
A sign on a Forest Service trail in northern Wisconsin marks this tree as a basswood. The Wisconsin DNR champion register adds the rest. It ranks it the biggest basswood in the state, with a trunk 4.09 metres round, a height of 36.6 metres, 120 feet, and a crown about 21 metres across.

The tree stands on the Assessor's Interpretive Trail, which starts at the east end of Lost Lake beside the campground in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest and runs through hemlocks and hardwoods past a series of interpretive signs. The same trail has a named tree of its own, the Assessor White Pine, worth looking for on the way.

For scale, the champion basswood of the Chicago forest preserves, on our Chicago page, is 3.91 metres round and 24.4 metres tall. This one is a little thicker and twelve metres taller, a basswood built for height.

The trail is free and open to walkers, and there is no public transport out here; Florence is the nearest town to drive from. The register is the only source for the tree and does not date its measurement. Nobody has published an age. If you know it, tell us.
